title: In an array where every number appears twice except two numbers that each appear once, find both single numbers using constant extra space. Explain how a distinguishing set bit splits the array into two groups.
shortTitle: Two Single Numbers (Find the Two Elements That Each Appear Once)

s1_definition.profdef: Two Single Numbers extends the XOR trick. XOR-ing the whole array gives the XOR of the two unpaired numbers, call it x. Because the two numbers differ, x has at least one set bit; we isolate its rightmost set bit and use it to partition the array into two groups, one where that bit is set and one where it is not. Each group contains exactly one of the singles, so XOR-ing within each group isolates them separately.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, two orphan reconciliation entries slipped through unmatched while everything else is paired. XOR-ing all codes gives the combined fingerprint of the two orphans. We pick one bit where they differ and sort every code into two buckets by that bit, so each orphan falls alone into its own bucket, and XOR-ing each bucket reveals it.
s1_definition.oneliner: XOR everything to combine the two singles, isolate a differing bit, split into two groups by that bit, and XOR each group to recover each single.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two Single Numbers extends the XOR trick. XOR-ing the whole array gives the XOR of the two unpaired numbers, call it x. Because the two numbers differ, x has at least one set bit; we isolate its rightmost set bit and use it to partition the array into two groups, one where that bit is set and one where it is not. Each group contains exactly one of the singles, so XOR-ing within each group isolates them separately.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, two orphan reconciliation entries slipped through unmatched while everything else is paired. XOR-ing all codes gives the combined fingerprint of the two orphans. We pick one bit where they differ and sort every code into two buckets by that bit, so each orphan falls alone into its own bucket, and XOR-ing each bucket reveals it.

**One line to remember:** XOR everything to combine the two singles, isolate a differing bit, split into two groups by that bit, and XOR each group to recover each single.

sections.s2_technical:
First we XOR the whole array into `x`, which equals the two singles XOR-ed together because all pairs cancel. Since the two singles are distinct, `x` is non-zero and has at least one set bit. We isolate the rightmost set bit with `int rightmostBit = x & -x;`, a classic two's-complement idiom. This bit is set in exactly one of the two singles, so it cleanly separates them.

Then we scan the array again, and for each number we test whether that bit is set: if `(num & rightmostBit) != 0` we XOR it into `num1`, otherwise into `num2`. For example, `if ((num & rightmostBit) != 0) num1 ^= num; else num2 ^= num;`. Within each group the paired values still cancel, leaving one single in `num1` and the other in `num2`.

A senior nuance is why `x & -x` isolates the rightmost set bit: negating in two's complement flips all bits and adds one, so ANDing the original with its negation keeps only the lowest set bit. Any set bit of `x` would work as the splitter; the rightmost is just the cheapest to compute. Complexity is O(n) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India found that two reconciliation entries, not one, were left unmatched while every other entry is paired, and operations must recover both orphan codes with constant extra space. This is exactly how Two Single Numbers works.

Problem 2 — A single XOR fold would only give the combined fingerprint of both orphans, not each one. This is why we isolate a bit where the two orphans differ and use it to split all codes into two buckets so each orphan is isolated in its own bucket.

The code defines a `DualOrphanService` exposing `findTwoOrphans(codes)` returning an int array of the two orphan codes. A `Demo` runs it over a batch with two orphans and logs both.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: codes 5001, 5002, 5003, 5002, 5001, 5009.

Step 1: XOR all codes. Paired 5001 and 5002 cancel, leaving x equal to 5003 XOR 5009, the combined fingerprint of the two orphans.

Step 2: Compute x AND negative-x to isolate the rightmost bit where 5003 and 5009 differ.

Step 3: Second pass. Each code is tested against that bit. 5003 lands in one bucket and 5009 in the other; every paired code cancels inside whichever bucket it falls into.

Step 4: num1 holds one orphan and num2 the other; we return 5003 and 5009.

```
Oct 27, 2026 11:04:19 PM com.bank.dual.service.DualOrphanService findTwoOrphans
INFO: Two unmatched codes = 5009 and 5003
INFO: Two orphans: [5009, 5003]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  codes:[5001,5002,5003,5002,5001,5009]
    │ pass 1: XOR all → x = 5003 ^ 5009
    ▼
  rightmostBit = x & -x   (a bit where they differ)
    │ pass 2: split by that bit
    ├─ bit set   bucket → XOR → 5009
    └─ bit clear bucket → XOR → 5003
    ▼
  [5009, 5003]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Two Single Numbers extends the basic XOR trick to the case where two elements each appear once. If I XOR the whole array, every pair cancels and I am left with the XOR of the two singles combined into one value. That combined value is not an answer by itself, but because the two singles are different numbers it must have at least one bit set, and any set bit is a bit where the two singles differ.

So I isolate one such bit, conventionally the rightmost set bit using the x-and-negative-x idiom from two's complement, and I use it as a splitter. I pass over the array a second time and route each number into one of two groups depending on whether that bit is set in it. The two singles are guaranteed to fall into different groups, while every paired value still cancels within whichever group it lands in, so XOR-ing each group independently hands me the two singles.

At the National Bank of India I used this when two reconciliation entries, rather than one, were left unmatched while everything else was paired, and the node had to recover both orphans with constant extra space. I XOR-ed all codes to get their combined fingerprint, isolated a differing bit, and partitioned the codes into two buckets so each orphan was isolated and revealed by XOR. Explaining the distinguishing-bit split and the rightmost-set-bit idiom is what shows an interviewer I can reason at the bit level under a space constraint.
